artifacts.title: Katawa Shoujo
artifacts.disability: Multiple disabilities (including visual, hearing and mobility impairments)
artifacts.focus: When does intimacy make a character more human—and when does an audience turn disability into an object of fascination?
artifacts.representation: Approach the visual novel as a tension between its adult-romance framing and its character-driven writing. The presence of intimacy is not itself evidence of exploitation; consider whether characters have choices, aspirations and disagreements beyond disability, and whether the story allows desire to be mutual rather than merely observed. Its global creators borrow a Japanese genre, so calling it straightforwardly “Eastern representation” would distort its production history.
artifacts.against: The game also packages disabled school-age characters within a dating-game structure. Even if it individualizes them, a player may still be encouraged to collect or classify routes through bodily difference. Analyze camera perspective, choice architecture and marketing separately from the writers’ stated intentions; academic commentators disagree over how successfully the work escapes fetishization. Discuss mature content without reproducing it.

artifacts.title: A Silent Voice
artifacts.focus: Can an apology-centered story still deny the harmed person control of the narrative?
artifacts.representation: Yoshitoki Ōima deliberately makes the former bully central and leaves parts of Shōko’s interior life inaccessible. This creates a film about the ethics of recognition and the difficulty of assuming we understand another person. Pay attention to the use of visual isolation, crowd markings and shifting conversational space.
artifacts.against: If the strongest perspective belongs to the person seeking forgiveness, disability risks becoming the moral obstacle someone else must overcome. Trace Shōko’s unprompted decisions rather than only the protagonist’s changes.

artifacts.title: Blind Massage (推拿)
artifacts.focus: How can cinema challenge a sighted audience’s assumption that seeing means knowing?
artifacts.representation: Lou Ye’s film makes work, touch, sound, attraction and aesthetic judgment inseparable from a community of blind massage therapists. artifacts.against: The film’s sensual attention can produce a more embodied account of desire, but can also expose its subjects to voyeuristic fascination. Analyze whose judgments of beauty and intimacy are heard rather than deciding that sensuality is automatically liberating or exploitative.

artifacts.title: Crip Camp
artifacts.focus: What is lost when disability politics is retold as a triumphant march toward legislation?

artifacts.title: Murderball
artifacts.focus: Does replacing pity with aggression redefine disability, or simply celebrate conventional masculinity?
artifacts.representation: The athletes are depicted as competitive, funny, flawed and physically ambitious. That roughness refuses the expectation that disabled subjects must be grateful or uplifting.
artifacts.against: Its focus on tough men also narrows who gets to embody independent disability. Compare the film’s language of athletic domination with REAL to see where sport expands and limits possible identities.

artifacts.title: I Didn’t See You There
artifacts.focus: What happens when a disabled filmmaker turns the camera away from himself?
artifacts.representation: Reid Davenport’s wheelchair-mounted and handheld footage rejects the demand that disabled people always be visually displayed for others’ comprehension. The technique transforms access, streets and public attention into a question about cinematic point of view.
artifacts.against: The film is not a universal portrait of disability; its refusal of the conventional talking-head format is itself a subjective aesthetic choice. Compare the gaze it rejects with Freaks and The Elephant Man.

artifacts.title: The Peanut Butter Falcon
artifacts.focus: When is representation transformed by writing a part around a disabled performer?
artifacts.representation: Zack Gottsagen performs a fictional protagonist with dreams, stubbornness and humor; filmmakers developed the project through their collaboration with him. This provides a concrete alternative to treating disability as merely an acting challenge for nondisabled stars.
artifacts.against: Road movies can still simplify support needs into a feel-good lesson for companions. Ask whether the character changes the plot or mainly gives the other men purpose.

artifacts.title: The Intouchables
artifacts.focus: What happens when disability, race and class are brought together as a friendship comedy?
artifacts.representation: Caregiving is presented through irreverence rather than sanctity, giving two men contrasting experiences of money, work and bodily dependence. Their humor makes interpersonal difference a source of mutual change.
artifacts.against: Roger Ebert’s criticism argues the film depends on reductive racial patterns. Examine whether it critiques systems of inequality or uses each man as a remedy for the other’s stereotyped deficiencies.

artifacts.title: The Good Doctor (US)
artifacts.focus: Does the autistic hero have to be a genius to be permitted in an elite workplace?
artifacts.representation: The U.S. medical drama, adapted from a Korean series, makes institutional prejudice part of its weekly plot. Shaun’s extraordinary diagnostic skill repeatedly earns him credibility with skeptical colleagues.
artifacts.against: Autistic commentators disagree: some value the professional visibility; others criticize narrow mannerisms and a lack of autistic creative control. Compare whose clinical needs the hospital meets with the conditional welcome it extends to Shaun.

artifacts.title: Speechless
artifacts.focus: Can a family sitcom let a nonspeaking teenager be sharp, difficult and funny without turning him into a lesson?
artifacts.representation: JJ is played by Micah Fowler, an actor with cerebral palsy. The family comedy uses assistive communication and daily conflicts as normal sitcom machinery, not just public-service instruction.
artifacts.against: The assertive mother can dominate the story’s voice, repeating the caregiver-centered format the show aims to transcend. Track when JJ shapes a joke or a decision and when others interpret him.

artifacts.title: Sex Education (Isaac storyline)
artifacts.focus: Can a disabled romantic character be flawed without his flaws being blamed on disability?
artifacts.representation: Isaac is played by George Robinson, a wheelchair user. The series makes him witty, protective and sometimes manipulative within a larger ensemble; this resists the expectation that disabled characters must always be model citizens.
artifacts.against: Authentic casting does not erase the question of how romantic conflict intersects with stereotypes of jealousy, dependence or desirability. Focus on authorship and audience judgment rather than treating intimate content as proof of progress.

artifacts.title: Hellblade: Senua’s Sacrifice
artifacts.focus: Can interactive design communicate distress without reducing psychosis to a supernatural mechanic?
artifacts.representation: Spatial audio, perception puzzles and consultation with people with lived experience and mental-health researchers make the game a case study in collaborative authorship. Its design frames differences in perception as part of play, not merely backstory.
artifacts.against: An evocative audiovisual approximation is not the same as everyone’s lived experience. Critique whether the game’s fantasy conventions clarify or blur the boundary between mental-health experience and horror aesthetics.

artifacts.title: The Vale: Shadow of the Crown
artifacts.focus: What if a game designed for blind players also reorganized how sighted players experience play?
artifacts.representation: Its audio-led interface and collaboration with blind and low-vision testers approach access as a design principle. The player’s blindness is not just a character trait: it alters the form of the game itself.
artifacts.against: Accessible mechanics do not automatically settle the representation of a fictional blind hero. Compare its sound-centered choices with visual substitutes for sight used by supernatural heroes like Daredevil.

artifacts.title: Flowers for Algernon
artifacts.focus: When does “becoming intelligent” expose the cruelty of society rather than the deficiency of the person?
artifacts.representation: Charlie’s written progress reports make literacy, social standing and the narrator’s changing self-understanding inseparable. The book offers a formal way to ask who sets standards for intelligence and human worth.
artifacts.against: The language of enhancement can still accept a hierarchy in which greater cognitive capacity earns humanity. Distinguish the 1959 short story from the expanded 1966 novel; the year 1969 in the original PDF is not the novel’s first publication date.

site.description: Forty real media works. Forty contested readings. Explore how disability, desire, access and authorship change across genres and places.
site.footerTitle: The story is never|the whole story.
site.footerText: Interpretations here are research starting points, not final judgments. Read the source, examine the original work, and look for disabled-led perspectives.
site.aboutBody: This research edition contains 40 case studies from multiple regions and media. Each entry makes an arguable claim, offers a counter-reading, and provides external research sources. The labels East and West are geographic browsing tools, not explanations of a culture. Katawa Shoujo is transnational and is intentionally marked Global.
